claims.text: At high temperatures, the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by in situ formation of a stable oxide layer.
The in situ oxide layer is lubricious.
The oxide layer shields the underlying metal from severe wear.
The baseline as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating has fine grains and minimal pre-oxidation.
Exposure to air at 600–800 °C during wear will promote oxide formation relative to room-temperature or inert-atmosphere testing.
A continuous, adherent oxide scale is the structural mediator of wear resistance.
High-temperature oxidative wear produces oxide species at the FeNiCrCoCu wear interface.
The interfacial oxide species are likely enriched in Fe, Cr, or Cu oxides.
The oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
Reduced metal-to-metal contact lowers friction and abrasive action.
The oxide layer's effectiveness depends on continuous formation and adhesion during wear.
Oxidative high-temperature tests will exhibit lower friction coefficients than room-temperature or inert-atmosphere tests.
Oxidative high-temperature tests will exhibit lower wear volumes than room-temperature or inert-atmosphere tests.
Microscopy will reveal a coherent oxide layer after high-temperature oxidative wear testing.
The proposed protective-oxidation mechanism applies approximately within 600–800 °C, where oxidation is sufficiently rapid.
The proposed mechanism applies only at loads that permit steady oxide formation rather than immediate catastrophic spallation.
Comparable friction and wear in oxygen-rich and inert atmospheres at the same temperature would falsify the proposed governing role of oxide formation.
Failure to observe a coherent protective oxide layer after oxidative testing would falsify the hypothesis.
